title: She Made Garbage Trucks Dance: The Unseen Labor Behind Mierle Ukeles's Art
summary: In 1969, a frustrated young mother and artist named Mierle Laderman Ukeles wrote a manifesto that reframed all the tedious, unpaid labor of daily life—scrubbing, diapering, tidying—as "maintenance art." It was a direct challenge to the art world's obsession with the singular, usually male, genius. As she bluntly tells the director of a new documentary, Maintenance Artist: "If I was a male artist, I wouldn't be making maintenance art." The film, now in theaters, traces Ukeles's decades-long practice of spotlighting marginal labor. Her most famous gig: artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation, a role she held for 40 years. She didn't just observe—she embedded herself, shaking hands with every one of the department's 10,000 workers, learning their names, and collaborating on performances. In one piece, she choreographed a ballet of garbage trucks and street sweepers. The documentary is peppered with revealing anecdotes. When excerpts of her manifesto appeared in Artforum, critic Lucy Lippard called her to ask, "Are you real, or did Jack Burnham make you up?" Ukeles also cites Richard Serra's monumental steel sculptures: they "came out of worlds of work—steel makers and shipbuilders. But who are the people? Who does this? There is only the unique artist. That's what bugged me." Her 1976 piece "I Make Maintenance Art One Hour Every Day" involved taking 700 Polaroid photos of maintenance workers in a Financial District skyscraper. The choice of Polaroid wasn't just aesthetic—it was strategic. To gain the workers' trust and assure them she wasn't a spy from union or management, she used a method that left no secret negatives. The resulting camaraderie is palpable in archival footage, where Ukeles and workers chat on a first-name basis. While most artist documentaries glorify individuals, Maintenance Artist portrays Ukeles as one node in a broader community. However, it largely sidesteps her life in Jerusalem and her teaching at the Bezalel Academy. Still, the film arrives at an opportune moment, as conversations about invisible labor and care work gain traction. It invites viewers to consider: what else goes unnoticed in our daily lives, and who are the real artists of the everyday?
why_it_matters: Ukeles’s art challenges us to see value in daily chores and custodial work, things that keep schools, homes, and cities running but often go unnoticed. By asking who we consider an artist or a hero, her story encourages young people to appreciate the invisible labor all around them.

background_read: In the late 1960s, as the feminist art movement gained momentum, Mierle Laderman Ukeles—a young mother and artist—wrote a manifesto that turned the idea of art on its head. She called the repetitive work of cleaning, feeding, and tidying “maintenance art,” arguing it was just as creative as the paintings and sculptures celebrated in museums.

Her ideas were later published in Artforum, a prestigious art magazine, catching the attention of critic Lucy Lippard, a leading voice in feminist art who was initially skeptical that Ukeles was real. Ukeles went on to become the artist-in-residence at the New York City Department of Sanitation, the massive city agency that handles garbage and cleaning. For decades, she collaborated with the workers, famously choreographing a performance with garbage trucks.

She also critiqued the work of Richard Serra, a famous sculptor whose giant steel pieces rely on industrial labor but credit only the lone artist. This contrast speaks to a broader issue: whose work is visible and valued? The new documentary arrives as society debates essential workers and care labor, roles that Ukeles championed long before they entered mainstream conversation.

perspectives.description: Ukeles’s maintenance art elevates and validates care work, giving a voice to sanitation workers and homemakers. Her decades-long engagement shows that art can meaningfully reshape how society values essential, often invisible labor—and has influenced later discussions about who truly keeps communities running.

Some argue that her art remains confined to the art world elite, and its impact on the actual working conditions of sanitation employees may be more symbolic than transformative. The documentary’s omission of her later years could also suggest that her most powerful work lies behind her, leaving questions about sustained relevance.

Ukeles’s practice fits into a long feminist tradition that blurs the line between public and private activity and rejects the separation of “high art” from everyday craft. Her work mirrors broader social struggles: whose labor is recognized, compensated, and remembered, and what qualifies as creative work.

As automation and the gig economy expand, the concept of maintenance and care will only grow in importance. Ukeles’s approach could inspire new forms of community-based art and labor activism that bridge creative expression with policy, prompting institutions to formally acknowledge the workers behind the scenes.
